topic: Haley Stevens crosses over: a Michigan Democrat endorses Republican Mike Rogers over Abdul El-Sayed, amid fights over an Israel ad and Muslim Brotherhood claims
question: Is Abdul El-Sayed an extremist whose campaign tolerates antisemitism, as Rogers and now Stevens say, or the target of an anti-Muslim smear built on family history and guilt by association?
summary:
On Nov. 1, two days before the election, Rep. Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost Michigan's August Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed and then endorsed him, appeared with Republican Mike Rogers at a Detroit church and endorsed him instead. She cited an Oct. 24 ad by Rebellion PAC, a group co-founded by Cenk Uygur, in which a shopper puts back eggs because the $7 is needed 'for killing Palestinians.' She called it antisemitic and also objected to El-Sayed's past campaigning with streamer Hasan Piker. El-Sayed says the ad 'was not made by me' and he disagrees with it, but would not 'play the condemn game.' Schumer called Stevens's move a 'despicable betrayal'; Trump praised her.

The endorsement lands on top of a month of Republican attacks tying El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood. The record is split. Some right-side claims are false: there is no evidence El-Sayed is a Brotherhood member, and FactCheck.org rated Rogers's charge that he 'believes America deserved 9/11' false. Others hold up: El-Sayed signed a 2012 letter backing Egypt's Brotherhood-led government, and his half-sister's posts contradict his flat 'No' on family ties. On the left, the ad's premise that Israel aid empties grocery carts does not survive arithmetic. Whether the ad is antisemitic, and whether Stevens's switch is principle or grievance, the evidence cannot settle.
verdict: Leans slightly left. Republicans' headline charges, that El-Sayed is a Brotherhood member or a 'jihadist' who thinks America deserved 9/11, are unsupported or false. But the right has real points the left waves away: El-Sayed signed a 2012 pro-Morsi letter, his family-ties denial is contradicted by his own half-sister, and an allied ad rests on an economic claim that is false. Whether the ad is antisemitic and whether Stevens's switch is principled are value judgments the meter does not settle.
verificationNote: Claims were checked against CBS's 60 Minutes fact-check, FactCheck.org, the Treasury Department's Jan. 13 designation release and two CRS reports on Israel aid, all read directly. The half-sister's posts come from the Washington Free Beacon, which broke them, and were confirmed as reported by CBS and Sinclair; the posts themselves were not viewed. The Washington Post (403), The Hill (403) and Michigan Advance (403) could not be read; JNS's article body was truncated. Stevens's statement on El-Sayed's Israel rhetoric is quoted from CBS and JNS, not a primary transcript. The per-person aid figure is our arithmetic.

left.label: A smear campaign, and a sore loser
left.framing: Republicans, short on an economic message, are closing on fear: calling a man who would be the first Muslim senator a 'jihadist' and Brotherhood agent on the strength of his mother's college years. El-Sayed did not make the grocery ad and said he disagrees with it. Stevens, bankrolled by AIPAC's super PAC in the primary, is relitigating a race she lost.
left.strongestPoint: The most damaging right-side charges are unsupported or false: no reporting, including the Free Beacon's, shows El-Sayed is a Brotherhood member, and FactCheck.org found Rogers's 'deserved 9/11' charge false. El-Sayed has said 'Of course I don't think 9/11 was justified.'
left.weakestPoint: El-Sayed answered 'No' when asked on Meet the Press whether his family had Brotherhood ties, yet his half-sister wrote 'My family has long been MB.' Defenders rarely address that, or the ad's false economics, and 'the condemn game' sits awkwardly with Democrats' 2022 demand that Trump disavow Nick Fuentes.

right.label: An extremist the Democrats won't confront
right.framing: El-Sayed backed a Muslim Brotherhood government in 2012, comes from a Brotherhood family he denies, campaigned with a streamer who said America deserved 9/11, and won't condemn an ad blaming Israel for grocery prices. Stevens, a lifelong Democrat, is putting country over party, and the Democrats' fury proves her point.
right.strongestPoint: Several specific points check out: El-Sayed signed the 2012 Morsi letter, his half-sister's posts contradict his denial, the U.S. has since designated the Egyptian Brotherhood a terrorist group, and the allied ad's premise is false.
right.weakestPoint: The closing message goes far past that record. Trump called El-Sayed a 'jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member' and Cruz a 'jihadist leprechaun' without evidence of membership, and Rogers's 9/11 charge was rated false. Holding a candidate to account for his mother's activism in the 1970s is guilt by family association.

facts.claim: Abdul El-Sayed is a member or committed supporter of the Muslim Brotherhood.
facts.evidence: CBS: Trump called El-Sayed a 'jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member'; Cruz said he 'is a passionate supporter of the Muslim Brotherhood.' Sinclair, reporting the Free Beacon's findings: 'there is no evidence El-Sayed himself was personally involved.' El-Sayed on Fox: 'I have never been a member of the Muslim Brotherhood, I never will be.'
facts.explanation: No outlet, including the right-leaning Free Beacon that broke the family story, has produced evidence of membership. 'Supporter' rests on a 2012 letter (graded separately) and his family. Treasury did designate the Egyptian branch for material support to Hamas on Jan. 13, 2026, so the group's current status is not in dispute; El-Sayed's link to it is.

facts.claim: El-Sayed's denial that his family has Muslim Brotherhood ties is contradicted by his half-sister's posts.
facts.evidence: Asked on Meet the Press whether he or his family had Brotherhood ties, El-Sayed answered 'No.' His half-sister Eman Abdelhadi, June 24, 2012, per the Free Beacon: 'My family has long been MB'; July 3, 2013: 'I have had family jailed for being a part of it.' CBS: the posts say their birth mother was active in the Brotherhood in Egypt in the early 1970s.
facts.explanation: The posts were reported by the Free Beacon and described by CBS and Sinclair; they were not viewed directly here. El-Sayed says he has not discussed his mother's past with her, which may explain the denial but does not make it accurate. The posts describe relatives, not El-Sayed, and are 13 years old.

facts.claim: In 2012, El-Sayed signed a letter supporting Egypt's Muslim Brotherhood-led government under Mohamed Morsi.
facts.evidence: CBS 60 Minutes fact-check: El-Sayed was among 46 Egyptian-Americans who signed a letter to Morsi after the Arab Spring urging him to act against allies of the previous authoritarian leader. Free Beacon: the letter called on the Brotherhood-led government to 'purge the media and police.'
facts.explanation: The signature is real; Rogers's phrasing that he 'wrote a letter in support for the Muslim Brotherhood' compresses it. Morsi was Egypt's elected president, the letter was addressed to him as head of state, and the U.S. did not designate any Brotherhood branch until 2026. El-Sayed was a medical student.

facts.claim: El-Sayed believes America deserved the 9/11 attacks.
facts.evidence: Rogers, Aug. 5: 'Never in a million years did I think that I would be running against someone who believes America deserved 9/11.' FactCheck.org: Rogers 'provided no evidence.' El-Sayed on Fox & Friends, April 7: 'Of course I don't think [9/11 was justified].' On Meet the Press, Aug. 9: 'So, yes, America didn't deserve 9/11.'
facts.explanation: The line comes from Hasan Piker's 2019 livestream remark, which Piker later retracted. El-Sayed did campaign with Piker and on April 7 said 'I'm not here to disavow people's views,' though he was not asked about 9/11 specifically. The association is real; the belief attributed to him is not.

facts.claim: Leading Republicans are using religious labels such as 'jihadist' against El-Sayed in their closing message.
facts.evidence: Cruz, Oct. 28 in Grosse Pointe Woods: 'My nickname for the guy is the jihadist leprechaun,' adding that if El-Sayed joined the Intelligence Committee 'there is a very real risk that Americans will die.' Trump, per Sinclair: 'If you look at the guy running in Michigan, he's a jihadist.'
facts.explanation: The quotes are confirmed across CBS and the Sinclair-owned station group. Republicans say the attacks are about ideology and the 2012 letter, not religion. Whether the labels are bigotry, as Sanders says, or hardball politics is a value judgment; that they were said is not in dispute.

corroboration.source: CBS News (Sanders on Face the Nation)

facts.claim: The grocery ad Stevens objected to was made by an independent group, not El-Sayed's campaign, and he has said he disagrees with it.
facts.evidence: Newsweek: El-Sayed spokesperson Roxie Richner said the ad is 'not affiliated in any way with the Abdul for Senate campaign.' El-Sayed, per CBS: 'I've already been clear that that ad was not made by me, and I do not agree with the contents of that ad.' He added: 'You guys love to play the condemn game.'
facts.explanation: The ad came from Rebellion PAC, co-founded by Cenk Uygur, whose nephew Piker campaigned with El-Sayed in April. Disagreeing is not the same as calling it antisemitic, which Stevens demanded; JNS headlined that he 'distances himself' but 'doesn't denounce it.' Whether that distinction matters is a value question.

facts.claim: U.S. military aid to Israel is a meaningful reason American families struggle with grocery costs.
facts.evidence: Ad script, per Newsweek: 'we have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians... Apparently it's costing us a lot of money to drop bombs on Gaza.' CRS: the 2016 MOU pledges '$38 billion in military aid,' or '$33 billion in FMF grants, plus $5 billion' for missile defense, over ten years.
facts.explanation: About $3.8 billion a year is roughly $11 per American; even the April 2024 supplemental's $8.7 billion would not change a household grocery bill. El-Sayed's own argument, that the country should 'keep that money here at home,' is a spending-priority claim, a values question. The ad is an ally's, not his, but it is the left-side claim at issue.

facts.claim: El-Sayed's campaign told Stevens she was not welcome at its final events before she switched.
facts.evidence: CBS: El-Sayed 'asked his primary rival... to stay away from remaining campaign events,' per two sources, first reported by Politico. El-Sayed said he 'would rather not distract.' Bridge Michigan: Rep. Debbie Dingell, who organized the unity event, said 'I'm the one who pulled it because it had become way too distracting.'
facts.explanation: Both accounts hold: El-Sayed's campaign asked her to stay away, and Dingell cancelled the joint appearance. The request came after Stevens publicly set conditions on Oct. 30, including an apology for his Israel statements, so 'disinvited' and 'set an ultimatum' describe the same sequence from different ends.

powerLens.thesis: The power test: how each party judges a politician who crosses over to endorse the other side depends on which side gains. In September 2024, Republican Liz Cheney endorsed Kamala Harris. Democrats called her a patriot; Trump's campaign dismissed her. Now a Democrat has crossed to the Republican, and the reactions have swapped.

precedent.what: Cheney said, 'Because of the danger that Donald Trump poses, not only am I not voting for Donald Trump,' but would vote for Harris. Harris campaign chair Jen O'Malley Dillon called her 'a patriot.' Trump spokesman Steven Cheung: 'Who is Liz Cheney and what does she do?'
precedent.mirror: A defeated member of one party endorses the other party's nominee, citing a threat she says outweighs party loyalty. Cheney had lost her 2022 primary after breaking with Trump; Stevens lost a primary centered on Israel. Both were cheered by the side they helped and condemned by the side they left.

flips.then: 2024: Trump's campaign dismissed Cheney's crossover with 'Who is Liz Cheney and what does she do?'
flips.now: Trump on Stevens: 'Haley said what few people are willing to say.' Rogers called it 'courage in politics.'

flips.then: 2024: Harris's campaign called Cheney 'a patriot who loves this country' for crossing party lines.
flips.now: Schumer: 'This is a despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens.' Michigan's party chair said she is 'not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future.'

powerLens.longRun: Strip out the parties and the durable question is whether a defeated candidate owes the nominee her support, or owes voters her honest judgment of him. Each side's answer tracks who benefits. The same goes for guilt by association: Democrats demanded Trump disavow Nick Fuentes in 2022, and Republicans now demand El-Sayed disavow Piker. Expect both standards to swap again.
powerLens.appliedToScore: Neither side gets reasoning credit for its view of crossover endorsements or disavowals, since each holds the opposite view when the roles reverse; that is reflected in the weakest points. The needle rests on present-tense facts: what El-Sayed signed and said, what his opponents claimed, and what the ad asserted.

pattern.thesis: The Michigan fight joins two trends of the last two cycles: Republicans attacking Muslim Democratic candidates as tied to terrorism, and Democratic primaries splitting over Israel, with heavy AIPAC-linked spending. Graded alone it looks like one candidate's baggage; in sequence the recurring question is where scrutiny of a candidate's record ends and suspicion of his religion begins.

campaigns.what: Rep. Andy Ogles asked DOJ to investigate denaturalizing Zohran Mamdani, citing his 'vocal support for terrorist organizations.' Immigration experts told PolitiFact they had seen no evidence he lied on his application.
AIPAC's super PAC spent more than $14 million against Rep. Jamaal Bowman, an Israel critic, who lost to George Latimer by 17 points.
An AIPAC-affiliated super PAC spent tens of millions backing Stevens, per Al Jazeera; El-Sayed attacked that spending in debates as 'the quid of $30 million spent by AIPAC.'

pattern.takeaway: The recurring question is whether a candidate is being judged on what he has signed and said or on his faith, family and allies. The one-off tell is anyone who treats this race as unique: either 'Stevens alone saw the truth' or 'just Islamophobia,' without mentioning both the 2012 letter and the false 9/11 charge.

notAdjudicable: Whether the Rebellion PAC ad is antisemitic or a crude but legitimate criticism of U.S. aid, which turns on how one reads tropes and intent rather than on facts.
Whether a defeated primary candidate owes the nominee her support or should follow her own judgment, a question about party loyalty versus conscience.
How far a candidate should be held responsible for the views of relatives, allies and outside groups he did not control, a judgment about fairness and accountability.
Whether U.S. military aid to Israel is a worthwhile use of federal money compared with domestic spending, a question of foreign-policy and budget priorities.
Whether 'disagree with' is an adequate response to an allied ad or only 'condemn' will do, which depends on what one thinks candidates owe affected communities.
biasWatch: The bias at work is guilt by association, applied selectively. Critics stack El-Sayed's mother, half-sister, Piker and Uygur into a portrait of the candidate; defenders wave off his own signature on the 2012 letter and his inaccurate denial as part of the same smear. Each side accepts association as evidence when it hurts the other. The tell: watch for anyone who cites a relative or ally as proof of what El-Sayed believes without quoting El-Sayed, or who calls every question about his record Islamophobia without saying which claims are true.
